newsitem.title: CANADA: Make sea adventurers pay, Canadian rescuers say.
newsitem.headline: Make sea adventurers pay, Canadian rescuers say.

text.p: It's all glory for balloonists and yachtsmen crossing the ocean until trouble strikes. Then it's the taxpayer who has to pay, a Canadian government agency complained in a report released this week.

The document, written by the government's Halifax Rescue Coordination Centre, suggested the possibility of requiring adventurers to post a cash bond to pay for search-and-rescue operations or at least to make these operations safer.
"Incidents have involved transatlantic balloon racers, rowers, single-engine planes and ... single-handed ocean racers," the report said.

"Many of these adventurous people believe the only risk is to themselves and they should be left to do as they please. Little thought seems to be given to the cost of a rescue operation or the risk to persons on the rescue units."

Despite the outrage some feel when affluent adventurers get government help, Canadian Coast Guard Search and Rescue Director Gary Sidock told Reuters on Tuesday the International Convention on Search and Rescue required its 56 member states to do rescues without requiring cash.
But he said more could be done to prevent mishaps.

In recent examples of cost to taxpayers, two Canadian helicopters, a C-130 Hercules transport plane and a Coast Guard cutter had to search for American millionaire balloonist Steve Fossett when he ran into trouble in January 1996 in his attempt to circle the globe.

Fossett tried yet again last week to make man's first nonstop trip around the world in a balloon but failed because of lack of fuel. He landed in India on Monday, setting records for time and distance in his six-day, 10,000-mile (16,000 km) adventure.

The Halifax report also cited the prestigious Europe1 Star Single Handed Transatlantic Race last June and July saying "17 of the 58 boats that started, or almost 30 percent, had to quit or were involved in distress situations."
It said that yachtsmen violated "one of the basic laws of the sea" when they sailed alone, since they were not keeping a lookout when they were sleeping or working below decks.
One way of reducing costs to governments would be to require race organisers to place support vessels strategically along the intended race route, the report suggested.
Argentine, Chilean and Australian navies have spent much of the past three weeks searching in the Antarctic region for solo sailers who capsized in the Vendee Globe round-the-world race.
Canadian Gerry Roufs is still missing after two weeks.
Sidock said that in addition to the costs involved, such operations endangered the lives of rescuers and made planes and vessels unavailable for rescues elsewhere.

"By international agreement, we cannot charge for genuine distress," Sidock said, noting that most of Europe and North America, along with Chile, Argentina and Australia were members of the convention.
But he added: "We want to prevent the incident from happening in the first place, so there'd be no cost and no risk."
